newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian forces say seized last royalist bastion.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian forces say seized last royalist bastion.

text.p: Cambodian government forces on Tuesday said they had seized the last town held by loyalists of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, but the prince and his loyalists disputed the report.
Government officials said the town of O'Smach fell on Tuesday afternoon and royalists were retreating from the area.
O'Smach was seized at 1.10 p.m. (0610 GMT) and royalist troops were fleeing the area, said Nuo Sam, first deputy governor of the northwest province of Siem Reap.

A senior military offical told Reuters the government forces, under the control of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, had captured O'Smach slightly later, at around 2 p.m. (0700 GMT), after a major offensive on Tuesday.
He said Hun Sen's troops had seized seven royalist tanks but had no information on any prisoners or casualties.
But Ranariddh and his loyalists disputed the claims and also said that there was no need to have a major stronghold to launch guerrilla warfare.
"I talked to (my general) this morning and he said we held the town," Ranariddh said in Bangkok upon his return from a trip to Manila.
"For guerrilla warfare, there is no need for a major stronghold," he added.
Royalist soldiers at the Thai border near O'Smach told reporters they still held the town and that 5,000 soldiers would soon arrive to reinforce the royalists.

"With our ally (the Khmer Rouge), we can begin sabotage operations in many areas, including some big towns in Cambodia," said Chorn Chareya, an assistant to Ranariddh's military commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay.
O'Smach, a town near the Thai border, was the last major stronghold of Ranariddh's ragged army, which has been battling the government forces since Hun Sen overthrew the prince on July 6.
Gun and mortar fire rocked O'Smach throughout the day, officials at the border said.
Hours earlier more than 20,000 civilians fled O'Smach into Thailand to escape the fighting.

Thai authorities said they opened gates at a checkpoint and allowed the civilians to walk across the border to Kab Choeng district late on Monday after government troops captured the strategic hill of Khao Laem five km (three miles) from O'Smach.
The refugees spent the morning at a border market two km (one mile) inside Thailand and later moved on foot to Huay Choeng, six km from the border.
The lines of fleeing Cambodians stretched along the entire six km from the market to Huay Choeng, witnesses said.
The Thai army had sent reinforcements into the area and sealed off the border in anticipation of Tuesday's fighting.
About 2,000 civilians remain in O'Smach, where Ranariddh's forces had dug in against Hun Sen's troops with assistance from the Khmer Rouge.
Major Yen Bunsrun of Ranariddh's army said earlier he was getting support from about 1,000 Khmer Rouge, Maoists who ruled Cambodia during the 1975-79 "Killing Fields" years.
Hun Sen has justified his power grab by accusing Ranariddh of smuggling weapons and bringing Khmer Rouge into Phnom Penh.
Ranariddh will have to face trial on those charges, as well as explaining his cooperation with Khmer Rouge in the fighting if he returns to Phnom Penh, Hun Sen said.
Ranariddh on Tuesday snubbed Hun Sen's offer to return on condition he face trial. "I'm not crazy," he told reporters in Manila, where he held talks with Philippine President Fidel Ramos.
